title: How to measure loop currents in scanning tunneling microscopy
authors: Victoire Morisseau, Luke C. Rhodes, Peter Wahl, Carolina A. Marques
abstract: The emergence of loop current phases, where spontaneous loops of orbital currents give rise to a weak local magnetic moments, has been proposed to exist in a number of quantum materials based on measurements that pick up weak signatures of time reversal symmetry breaking or small magnetic moment order. The most prominent example is as an explanation of the pseudogap phase on the underdoped side of the phase diagram of the high-temperature cuprate superconductors, but more recently, it has been proposed to occur in Kagome materials and at the surface layer of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$. Experimental results have, however, been inconclusive so far, some detecting signatures that can be understood as emerging due to loop current phases, whilst others have not detected any significant proof. One of the techniques that should be able to pick up local signatures of loop current orders is low temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS), however firm predictions of how to detect them are missing. Here, we provide specific predictions for how loop current orders in a square lattice can be seen in spectroscopic maps, using models of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors and of the surface layer of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$. We find that, besides lifting degeneracies at the specific ordering vector of the loop current order, a finite spin polarisation emerges when spin-orbit coupling is present, signatures of which can be detected in spin-polarised STM.
summary: This work provides theoretical predictions for detecting loop current orders—spontaneous orbital currents—in quantum materials like cuprates and $	ext{Sr}_2	ext{RuO}_4$. By simulating STM/STS measurements on tight-binding models, the authors show that such order manifests as measurable spectral gaps in the DOS and characteristic patterns in QPI maps. These predictions guide future experimental efforts to confirm this exotic form of electronic ordering.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop specific theoretical predictions for how loop current orders, which break time-reversal symmetry, can be detected using low temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscopy and Spectroscopy (STM/STS) in quantum materials.
main_result: Loop currents are predicted to cause a splitting of Van Hove singularities (VHS) in the local density of states (DOS), leading to partial energy gaps ($\sim 10-20 	ext{ meV}$), and they predict the emergence of measurable spin polarization detectable by spin-polarized STM.
method: The authors use continuum Green's function methods applied to tight-binding models, simulating spectroscopic maps (LDOS) and Quasi-Particle Interference (QPI) patterns for both cuprates and $	ext{Sr}_2	ext{RuO}_4$.
model_or_system: The study applies theoretical modeling to high-temperature cuprate superconductors and the surface layer of $	ext{Sr}_2	ext{RuO}_4$, incorporating loop current terms ($\hat{H}_{	ext{LC}}$) into tight-binding Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Spectroscopic maps (DOS), QPI patterns with characteristic scattering vectors, and finite spin polarization detectable by spin-polarized STM.
important_parameters: Loop current strength ($m$), energy gap size ($\Delta E \sim 10-20 	ext{ meV}$), and the presence/absence of Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC).
main_assumptions: The calculations simplify by assuming staggered loop currents across the unit cell, and they neglect potential self-energy effects accompanying the order formation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate DOS splitting and QPI changes in both cuprate and $	ext{Sr}_2	ext{RuO}_4$ models as a function of loop current strength ($m$), alongside predicted spin polarization maps for SP-STM detection.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context (loop currents in superconductors), details the theoretical framework using tight-binding models, and then presents specific predictions regarding observable signatures—namely DOS splitting, QPI changes, and spin polarization—for both cuprates and ruthenates.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter physics, the detailed mapping of symmetry breaking (time-reversal symmetry) to measurable spectroscopic fingerprints is highly relevant to understanding emergent order parameters in strongly correlated systems, which shares conceptual links with many-body dynamics studied in AMO contexts.
